newsitem.title: USA: GM's Oldsmobile sees '97 sales decline.
newsitem.headline: GM's Oldsmobile sees '97 sales decline.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s Oldsmobile Division will mark its centennial in 1997 with another sales decline, but new models should fuel a rebound starting in 1998, executives said Thursday.

Oldsmobile General Manager John Rock told reporters at a news briefing here that the division's total sales in the 1997 calendar year will fall to 330,000 vehicles from about 340,000 to 350,000 in 1996.
Sales fell to 387,545 cars and trucks in 1995. The 1997 projection would be the division' poorest showing since 1961.
Oldsmobile, founded in August 1897, is the oldest surviving nameplate in the U.S. auto industry, but its sales have declined steadily since their peak in 1985 at 1.07 million units.
Summing up Olds' situation for 1997, Rock said, "The good news is the new cars are here. The bad news is the new cars are here."

Although the new models, including the Silhouette minivan, the all-new Cutlass mid-size sedan and the Intrigue mid-size sedan, will breathe new life into Oldsmobile's aging product line, the model changeovers will limit production and availability of cars.
As it rolls out the new models, Olds plans to cut back on low-profit fleet sales and aims to increase its retail sales in 1997 to 265,000 units from an anticipated 240,000 units this year.

He said Oldsmobile won't show its true capabilities until 1999, when its product line has been completely replaced. Retail sales in 1998 should exceed 300,000 units, and they could reach 350,000 to 450,000 units in 1999, depending on the economy.
But Olds has to successfully change its image to attract import buyers for the strategy to be successful.

"If you just keep thinking about Oldsmobile as big old luxoboats and traditional domestic cars and a great alternative to a Buick, then I've wasted a lot of time and a lot of the company's money," Rock said.
He added that the division is "introducing a product line to be reckoned with."

The first of the new products to reach showrooms will be the Silhouette minivan this fall. The van is the most upscale of GM's three new U.S. minivans and will start at around $20,000, said Silhouette/Bravada brand manager Michael McEnaney.
He added that Olds plans to sell about 20,000 to 25,000 Silhouettes annually, compared to expected 1996 sales of less than 8,000 of the current, plastic-bodied Silhouette vans.

GM in November will start production of the Oldsmobile Cutlass, a new mid-size sedan that recycles the division's most successful nameplate. With an expected price tag between $15,000 and $20,000, the car is designed to compete with the Honda Accord and Toyota Camry.
Olds officials say the top-end Cutlass, with a V-6 engine, automatic transmission and leather seats, will be price competitive with a base four-cylinder Camry.
In February 1997, GM will start production of the 1998 Oldsmobile Intrigue, a slightly larger, more stylish sedan priced in the low- to mid-$20,000 range.

The car replaces the current Cutlass Supreme. Oldsmobile officials said Thursday that the car will use GM's mainstay 3.8-liter V-6 engine instead of a 24-valve 3.4-liter V-6 previously earmarked for the car.

In 1998, Oldsmobile will get replacements for the compact Achieva and the 88 Royale large car. The Alero will be slightly smaller than the Cutlass, while the Antares will become Olds' new entry-level luxury car, priced between the Intrigue and the $35,000 Aurora flagship sedan.

"Picture a car lineup with an Accord, a Camry, a Maxima, an entry level luxury car and a Lexus LS400, and oh, by the way, we've also got a minivan and a sport utility," said Ken Stewart, Intrigue/Cutlass Supreme brand manager.
